strengths: The retrieval interface is practically useful: agents can combine dense and lexical retrieval, target entities, and manage retrieved context through a lightweight implementation.
Results cover six QA benchmarks. The same-backbone Qwen2.5-7B comparison reports average EM improving from 43.1 for Search-R1 to 47.5, providing positive evidence beyond the headline comparison.
Training-free experiments and SFT/RL ablations support the usefulness of the workflow and training stages. The appendix provides prompts and several implementation details.
weaknesses: The evaluation corpus is benchmark-conditioned. Appendix C.3 selects documents using benchmark evidence metadata and, for datasets such as Bamboogle, queries generated from questions and ground-truth answers. This introduces answer-informed corpus selection and weakens claims about realistic retrieval and generalization. A fixed, independently constructed corpus is needed, even if all methods share the curated corpus.

The central ablation does not isolate adaptive retrieval control: removing interaction also removes lexical retrieval, entity matching, and additional evidence access. Missing comparisons include fixed hybrid retrieval, query-only agents using the same hybrid backend, and individual primitive ablations under matched context budgets.

The headline 22.5% improvement compares Qwen3-8B against Qwen2.5-7B trained baselines. Appendix B.1 partially addresses this, but training data and optimization remain unmatched, limiting attribution of gains to the proposed interface.

Novelty is primarily the integration of established retrieval operations, planner/reasoner/executor prompting, and standard SFT plus GRPO. The broad claim that existing agentic retrieval is confined to semantic query reformulation is insufficiently established against prior tool-based search and retrieval-control approaches.

Efficiency is measured only through interaction counts, although one interaction can perform multiple searches and return extra entity snippets. Without latency, token usage, retrieval-operation counts, or matched evidence budgets, fewer turns do not establish lower computational cost.

Evaluation reliability and reproducibility need clarification. There are no uncertainty estimates or reported repeated runs; RL dynamics are measured on test subsets without explaining checkpoint-selection safeguards; and the RL training-set size differs between Section 4 and Appendix C.1. Several EM values also do not match the increments implied by the stated evaluation sizes, requiring an explanation of averaging or scoring.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful practical problem: allowing RAG agents to control retrieval beyond query reformulation. The proposed interface combines dense and lexical retrieval, entity matching, and context management using relatively lightweight infrastructure.

Reported results are promising across six QA benchmarks. The same-backbone Qwen2.5-7B comparison in Table 4 achieves 47.5 average EM versus 43.1 for Search-R1, providing positive evidence beyond the stronger-backbone comparison in the main table.

The paper evaluates both trained and training-free variants. Ablations support the utility of the combined interaction capabilities, SFT, and RL, while the appendix provides prompts, implementation details, and several training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The evaluation corpus raises a substantial validity concern. Appendix C.3 describes selecting documents using benchmark evidence metadata and, for datasets without explicit evidence, generating retrieval queries from both questions and ground-truth answers. The resulting 280,000-chunk corpus is therefore informed by the evaluation targets rather than independently constructed. This does not establish direct answer exposure to the agent, but it changes retrieval difficulty and weakens claims about standard open-domain performance and generalization. Evaluation on a fixed, answer-independent corpus is needed.

The central ablation does not isolate adaptive retrieval control from stronger retrieval infrastructure. Removing interaction also removes lexical search, entity matching, fusion, and context controls, leaving only dense retrieval. Consequently, the gains could largely reflect access to better retrieval tools. Missing controls include fixed hybrid retrieval, a query-only agent backed by the same hybrid retriever, and individual primitive ablations under comparable evidence budgets.

The headline 22.5% improvement compares Interact-RAG using Qwen3-8B against Search-R1 using Qwen2.5-7B, confounding the method with backbone capability. Appendix B.1 partially addresses this and remains encouraging, but the relative gain falls to approximately 10.1%. Training data and optimization also differ, so the main comparison cannot attribute the full improvement to the proposed interaction paradigm.

The novelty is insufficiently established relative to the breadth of the claims. The engine exposes familiar dense retrieval, BM25, weighted fusion, term matching, and filtering operations; the workflow and SFT-to-GRPO pipeline also use established components. A useful integration is possible, but the paper needs stronger positioning against hybrid retrieval and tool-using agents, and evidence that learned control contributes beyond these existing ingredients. Describing prior agentic RAG generally as confined to black-box semantic search is overly broad.

Efficiency claims rely on interaction counts rather than comparable computational costs. One Interact-RAG turn can execute multiple retrieval operations and append additional entity-matched snippets, while the workflow invokes multiple LLM modules. Without latency, generated and retrieved token counts, backend calls, and matched-budget comparisons, fewer turns do not establish lower overall cost.

Experimental reliability and reproducibility remain incomplete. Evaluation uses only 500 examples per dataset, or 125 for Bamboogle, without confidence intervals or repeated-run results. Figure 4 monitors a subset of the test datasets during training, but checkpoint-selection procedures and independent validation are unspecified. The custom corpus and sampled evaluation IDs are especially important for reproduction. Reporting inconsistencies, including 7.1K versus 7.4K RL examples and the training-step units in Figure 4, further impede verification. Together with the evaluation and attribution concerns, these weaknesses place the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The agent-controlled retrieval interface is practically motivated and implementable: it combines dense and lexical retrieval, entity matching, adaptive fusion, and context management using lightweight infrastructure.
Reported results are promising across six QA benchmarks. The same-backbone Qwen2.5-7B comparison strengthens the evidence, improving average EM from Search-R1’s 43.1 to 47.5.
Ablations support contributions from interaction, SFT, and RL. The training-free workflow also improves over MA-RAG on all three evaluated datasets.
The appendix provides useful implementation details, training settings, and workflow prompts.
weaknesses: The evaluation corpus is conditioned on benchmark evidence and, for datasets without explicit evidence, queries synthesized from questions and ground-truth answers (Appendix C.3). This introduces answer-informed corpus selection and substantially changes the retrieval setting. Even if shared across methods, it limits conclusions about realistic retrieval and generalization; evaluation on a fixed, independently constructed corpus is needed.

The central ablation does not isolate adaptive agent control from stronger retrieval infrastructure. Removing interaction also removes lexical search, entity matching, and additional evidence access. Missing controls include fixed hybrid retrieval and query-only agents using the same retrieval backend and context budget, alongside individual primitive ablations.

The headline 22.5% improvement compares Qwen3-8B against trained Qwen2.5-7B baselines. The appendix partially addresses this confound, but training data, supervision, and retrieval budgets remain unmatched, preventing clean attribution of the gains.

Novelty is primarily a combination of established retrieval operations, planner–reasoner–executor prompting, and standard SFT/GRPO training. The broad claim of a new paradigm requires stronger positioning against hybrid retrieval and agents with richer search tools.

Efficiency is measured only through interaction counts. Each interaction can execute multiple retrieval operations, append entity snippets, and vary context size, so fewer turns do not establish lower latency or computational cost. Token counts, retrieved context volume, and wall-clock measurements are missing.

Evaluation uses small sampled subsets without uncertainty estimates or repeated-run results. Reproducibility is further weakened by inconsistent RL dataset sizes (7.1K versus 7.4K), unspecified sampling seeds and score-normalization details, and unclear checkpoint-selection procedures despite monitoring test subsets during training.

strengths: The retrieval interface is practically useful: combining dense and lexical search, entity-focused snippets, document filters, and adjustable context gives agents meaningful control over evidence gathering.
Reported improvements are substantial even with a matched backbone: Interact-RAG-7B achieves 47.5 average EM versus Search-R1's 43.1, with particularly strong gains on 2Wiki and MuSiQue.

The evaluation includes six QA benchmarks, an additional news-domain benchmark, supporting-fact coverage, training-free execution, and component ablations. These provide several complementary indications that the system is effective.

The appendix provides useful implementation details, prompts, training settings, and latency measurements. The authors acknowledge the increased inference cost rather than relying exclusively on retrieval-iteration counts.
weaknesses: The evaluation corpus raises a major validity concern. Appendix D.3 reveals that the experiments use a curated 280,000-chunk corpus assembled from benchmark evidence and, for datasets without explicit evidence, queries generated using questions and ground-truth answers. This introduces answer-informed corpus selection and substantially changes the claimed Wikipedia retrieval setting. Sharing this corpus across methods helps internal comparison but does not establish performance on an independently constructed corpus. Evaluation without test-answer-informed corpus construction is needed.

The central claim about adaptive interaction is insufficiently isolated. The method gains access to BM25, entity snippets, and variable retrieval budgets, whereas the query-only comparison uses dense retrieval. Removing these capabilities together cannot distinguish learned interaction from simply providing a stronger retriever. A fixed hybrid-retrieval baseline, static entity augmentation, and agents compared under matched evidence budgets are essential controls. Table 8 compares fusion rules but does not resolve this issue.

The headline 22.5% improvement compares Qwen3-8B against a Qwen2.5-7B Search-R1 checkpoint. The matched 7B results are valuable and mitigate this concern, but training data, teacher supervision, and optimization remain unmatched. The paper therefore cannot attribute the headline improvement specifically to its proposed interaction paradigm.

Novelty is primarily in system integration. The retrieval primitives, planner–reasoner–executor decomposition, successful-trajectory SFT, and GRPO are established techniques. The broad characterization of prior agents as confined to semantic query reformulation is insufficiently substantiated, and the paper does not adequately position its contribution against agents with lexical search, entity lookup, filtering, or other structured retrieval tools.

Statistical reliability and reporting require clarification. Most datasets contain only 500 sampled evaluation questions, and no confidence intervals or seed variation are reported, making small primitive-ablation differences difficult to interpret. Several Bamboogle EM values are incompatible with a single binary exact-match evaluation over the stated 125 questions unless an unreported averaging procedure was used. Other inconsistencies include 7.1K versus 7.4K RL examples, incorrect MuSiQue percentage drops in Table 2, and a training axis labeled in thousands despite an approximately 110-step run. Training curves also use test subsets without clarifying whether checkpoint selection was independent.

The efficiency evidence supports fewer retrieval iterations, not lower overall inference cost: Table 7 reports 36.4 seconds for Interact-RAG versus 17.2 seconds for Search-R1, with substantially more generated tokens. The additional Best-of-3 comparison lacks a specified answer-selection procedure, and the paper does not establish performance under matched total compute budgets.

strengths: The retrieval interface is practical and clearly motivated: combining dense retrieval, lexical search, entity matching, and context management gives agents useful additional capabilities.
Table 1 reports meaningful improvements, including a same-backbone comparison: Interact-RAG-7B achieves 47.5 average EM versus 43.1 for Search-R1-7B.

The evaluation includes component and training ablations, training-free experiments, supporting-fact coverage, a non-Wikipedia benchmark, and explicit latency measurements. These provide useful evidence beyond final answer accuracy.
weaknesses: The evaluation corpus raises a substantial validity concern. Appendix D.3 constructs it using benchmark evidence metadata and, for datasets without explicit evidence, queries generated from both questions and ground-truth answers. This answer-informed corpus construction changes the retrieval task and potentially favors answer-specific lexical matching. Sharing the corpus across methods does not establish performance on an independently constructed corpus; an answer-independent evaluation is needed.

The central contribution is not adequately isolated. Removing interaction also removes lexical retrieval, entity snippets, and context controls. There is no strong fixed hybrid-retrieval baseline with comparable evidence access and context budgets, or baseline agent equipped with the same tools. Consequently, the gains do not establish that adaptive manipulation is superior to simply providing a stronger retrieval backend. Table 8's fusion comparisons do not resolve this.

The headline 22.5% improvement compares Qwen3-8B against Qwen2.5-7B checkpoints, confounding the method with backbone differences. The same-backbone results are encouraging but smaller, and training data, teacher supervision, and training budgets remain unmatched. Existing checkpoints are also evaluated on a newly constructed retrieval environment without corresponding adaptation.

Novelty is primarily in system integration. Hybrid retrieval, keyword/entity matching, document filtering, planner–reasoner–executor workflows, SFT, and GRPO are established components. The paper does not sufficiently position its interface against prior tool-based retrieval systems to justify the broad claim of a new paradigm.

Fewer interaction rounds do not establish greater computational efficiency: Table 7 reports 36.4 seconds for Interact-RAG versus 17.2 seconds for Search-R1, with substantially more generated tokens. The Best-of-3 comparison is useful but leaves the selection procedure unspecified and does not provide a systematic matched-compute comparison.

Experimental uncertainty and reproducibility remain insufficient. Most evaluations use only 500 examples, or 125 for Bamboogle, without confidence intervals or repeated-run variability; several primitive-ablation differences are very small. The paper does not clearly specify whether ablated agents are retrained, reports conflicting RL dataset sizes of 7.1K and 7.4K, and monitors a subset of test datasets during training without clarifying checkpoint selection. These gaps weaken confidence in the claimed component effects and generalization.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: enabling RAG agents to control lexical/dense retrieval, entity matching, and context selection. The interaction engine is concrete and reasonably lightweight.

Reported improvements are substantial. On the matched Qwen2.5-7B backbone, Interact-RAG achieves 47.5 average EM versus Search-R1’s 43.1, outperforming it on five of six benchmarks. The additional news-domain evaluation provides encouraging transfer evidence.

The evaluation includes component ablations, training-free experiments, supporting-fact coverage, action-use analysis, and latency measurements. Removing interaction reduces performance across all three ablation datasets, supporting the usefulness of the expanded retrieval interface.
The appendix provides implementation details, training hyperparameters, and workflow prompts, and candidly reports the increased inference cost.
weaknesses: The evaluation corpus construction materially limits the main claims. Appendix D.3 describes a benchmark-specific corpus assembled using candidate evidence and, for datasets without explicit evidence, synthetic queries derived from questions and ground-truth answers. This introduces answer-informed corpus selection and differs substantially from the generic Wikipedia setting described in Section 4.1. Sharing this corpus across methods preserves some comparative value, but does not establish performance in realistic open-corpus retrieval. Evaluation on a fixed corpus constructed independently of test answers is needed.

The experiments do not adequately isolate adaptive interaction from access to stronger retrieval tools. The main interaction ablation removes lexical retrieval, entity snippets, and context controls together. A query-only agent using a fixed hybrid retriever with the same entity information and context budget is missing. Table 8 compares fusion rules within the full system, but does not establish that learned retrieval control is necessary. This is especially important because the primitives, planner/reasoner/executor decomposition, and SFT-plus-GRPO training are largely established components.

The headline 22.5% improvement compares Qwen3-8B against Qwen2.5-7B checkpoints, conflating backbone and method improvements. The matched 7B results are valuable, but training data, teacher supervision, and optimization remain unmatched. The paper also disables native thinking for some prompted baselines. Stronger controlled comparisons are needed to attribute the gains to the proposed contribution.

Statistical and model-selection details are insufficient. Most evaluations use only 500 sampled examples, with 125 for Bamboogle, yet no confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are reported. Section 4.5 evaluates training progress on subsets of the test datasets without explaining whether these informed checkpoint selection. The RL dataset size also differs between Section 4.1 and Appendix D.1, and Figure 4 labels training steps in thousands despite the appendix describing roughly 110 steps.

Fewer retrieval iterations should not be interpreted as lower overall inference cost. Table 7 reports 36.4 seconds per question versus Search-R1’s 17.2 seconds, with substantially more generated tokens. The appendix acknowledges this tradeoff, but the main efficiency narrative overemphasizes iteration counts. The Best-of-3 comparison is helpful but lacks a specified answer-selection procedure and a full matched-budget comparison.
